---
title: "Learning Embeddings: from PCA to Deep Networks"
---

Chapter 2 treats an embedding as a finished object and asks what its geometry
means. This chapter asks the prior question: where does the embedding come from?
Every embedding is the solution to an optimization problem. A model is trained to
place biological entities in a low-dimensional space so that a chosen objective —
reconstruction, co-occurrence prediction, likelihood, or instance discrimination —
is minimized or maximized. The design choices that matter most are the choice of
objective and the data it is evaluated on, not the size of the network. The
chapter moves from objectives that admit closed-form or convex solutions (matrix
factorization, spectral methods) to shallow neural predictors (word2vec, GloVe,
node2vec), to reconstruction-based deep models (autoencoders, variational
autoencoders), to the contrastive and masked-prediction objectives that underpin
modern biological foundation models.

Following Appendix A, vectors are bold lowercase ($\mathbf{x}$, $\mathbf{z}$),
matrices are bold uppercase ($\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{W}$), scalars are italic
($n$, $d$, $k$, $\tau$), model parameters are collected in $\theta$, and the
$\ell_2$ norm is $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$. A data matrix is
$\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ with rows $\mathbf{x}_1,\dots,\mathbf{x}_n$;
an embedding is $\mathbf{z}_i\in\mathbb{R}^{k}$ with $k\ll d$; $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$
is the inner product, $\sigma(t)=1/(1+e^{-t})$ is the logistic sigmoid, and
$D_{\mathrm{KL}}$ and $I$ denote the Kullback--Leibler divergence and mutual
information.

# Matrix Factorization and Spectral Methods

The oldest learned embeddings come from linear algebra. They need no gradient
descent and no dataset beyond a matrix of observations or similarities.

::: {.callout-note}
## Definition
**Latent space.** A latent space is a lower-dimensional coordinate system
$\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^k$ inferred from observed data $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ with
$k \ll d$, chosen so that the coordinates retain the structure the objective
rewards. An embedding is the map $\mathbf{x} \mapsto \mathbf{z}$ together with the
coordinates it produces.
:::

## Principal Component Analysis and the Eckart--Young Theorem

Given a centered data matrix $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$ with rows
$\mathbf{x}_1,\dots,\mathbf{x}_n$, sample mean
$\bar{\mathbf{x}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{x}_i$, and sample covariance
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\mathbf{x}_i-\bar{\mathbf{x}})(\mathbf{x}_i-\bar{\mathbf{x}})^\top$,
principal component analysis (PCA) [@pearson1901lines] seeks an orthonormal
projection $\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}$ with
$\mathbf{W}^\top\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{I}_k$ solving

$$
\mathbf{W}^\star
= \arg\max_{\mathbf{W}^\top \mathbf{W} = \mathbf{I}_k} \; \operatorname{tr}\!\left(\mathbf{W}^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \mathbf{W}\right)
\;=\; \arg\min_{\mathbf{W}^\top \mathbf{W} = \mathbf{I}_k} \; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left\lVert (\mathbf{x}_i-\bar{\mathbf{x}}) - \mathbf{W} \mathbf{W}^\top (\mathbf{x}_i-\bar{\mathbf{x}}) \right\rVert_2^2,
$$ {#eq-ch03-pca}

where $\mathbf{I}_k$ is the $k \times k$ identity and the $k$ columns of
$\mathbf{W}$ are the leading principal directions. Object (@eq-ch03-pca) states the
same optimizer $\mathbf{W}^\star$ two ways: it maximizes the
projected variance on the left and minimizes the residual reconstruction error on
the right, and the two problems have the same solution because the total variance is fixed. To see the
equivalence, use the orthogonality identity
$\lVert(\mathbf{x}_i-\bar{\mathbf{x}}) - \mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^\top(\mathbf{x}_i-\bar{\mathbf{x}})\rVert_2^2
= \lVert \mathbf{x}_i-\bar{\mathbf{x}}\rVert_2^2 - \lVert \mathbf{W}^\top(\mathbf{x}_i-\bar{\mathbf{x}})\rVert_2^2$,
which holds whenever $\mathbf{W}^\top\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{I}_k$; summing over $i$ and
dividing by $n$ shows that the residual is
$\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) - \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{W}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{W})$,
so minimizing the residual is the same as maximizing the retained variance. The
Eckart--Young theorem states that this optimum, and the best rank-$k$ approximation
of any matrix in the Frobenius norm, is obtained by truncating the singular value
decomposition [@eckart1936approximation]. PCA is therefore a learned embedding whose
coordinates are the projections $\mathbf{z}_i = \mathbf{W}^\top(\mathbf{x}_i-\bar{\mathbf{x}})$,
and it remains the canonical baseline whenever a new embedding claims to capture
biological signal. Its assumptions are a linear subspace, centered isotropic
noise, and a squared error that penalizes large residuals; it fails, in the sense
of capturing little variance, when the data lie on a curved manifold or when
variance along a direction is dominated by an uninformative nuisance factor such as
batch.

## Latent Semantic Analysis

Latent semantic analysis (LSA) applies the same factorization to a sparse
term--document count matrix, weighting counts and truncating the singular value
decomposition to embed terms and documents in a shared space [@deerwester1990indexing].
Its biological analogues replace terms and documents with biological pairs: genes
and samples, codons and proteins, or nodes and contexts. LSA shows the central
pattern that recurs throughout the chapter — an embedding can be read off any
large co-occurrence matrix whose low-rank structure is meaningful.

## Spectral Embedding

Spectral methods embed the vertices of a graph directly. Given a symmetric
affinity matrix $\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ with $W_{ij} \geq 0$
(following Appendix A's overloading of this letter, $\mathbf{W}$ here is graph
affinity, not the PCA projection above), degree matrix
$\mathbf{D} = \operatorname{diag}(D_{11},\dots,D_{nn})$ with
$D_{ii} = \sum_j W_{ij}$, and graph Laplacian $\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{D} - \mathbf{W}$,
Laplacian eigenmaps choose coordinates $\mathbf{y}_1,\dots,\mathbf{y}_n \in \mathbb{R}^k$,
stacked as the rows of $\mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}$, minimizing

$$
\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j} W_{ij} \left\lVert \mathbf{y}_i - \mathbf{y}_j \right\rVert_2^2
= \operatorname{tr}\!\left(\mathbf{Y}^\top \mathbf{L}\, \mathbf{Y}\right)
\quad \text{subject to} \quad \mathbf{Y}^\top \mathbf{D}\, \mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{I}_k,
$$ {#eq-ch03-laplacian}

where the rows of $\mathbf{Y}$ are the vertex embeddings and the factor
$\tfrac12$ is the usual convention that makes the two sides equal (the objective is
defined only up to a positive constant) [@belkin2003laplacian]. The equality is the
identity $\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}W_{ij}\lVert\mathbf{y}_i-\mathbf{y}_j\rVert_2^2
= \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{Y}^\top(\mathbf{D}-\mathbf{W})\mathbf{Y})$; the
constraint $\mathbf{Y}^\top\mathbf{D}\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{I}_k$ prevents collapse to
the trivial solution, and the optimizer is obtained from the smallest generalized
eigenvectors of $(\mathbf{L}, \mathbf{D})$ after discarding the constant
eigenvector. The objective is minimized over $\mathbf{Y}$, and it penalizes large
displacement across heavily weighted edges, so the embedding is smooth over the
graph. This formulation is the direct ancestor of the graph neural networks in
Chapter 10 and of the random-walk objectives below.

# Shallow Prediction Methods

A second family keeps the objective stochastic: instead of factoring a fixed
matrix, the model predicts one entity from another observed nearby and is trained
by gradient descent on mini-batches.

## word2vec

word2vec learns vectors by predicting context. The continuous bag-of-words
(CBOW) variant predicts a center word from its context, while skip-gram predicts
context words from a center word [@mikolov2013efficient]. Training with full
softmax is expensive, so the skip-gram with negative sampling (SGNS) objective
replaces it with binary classification between observed and sampled pairs. Let
$\mathbf{u}_w \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ and $\mathbf{v}_c \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ be the input
("center") and output ("context") vectors of word $w$ and context $c$,
$\mathcal{D}$ the set of observed (center, context) pairs, $K$ the number of
negatives, and $P_n$ a smoothed unigram noise distribution. SGNS maximizes

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{SGNS}}(\{\mathbf{u}\},\{\mathbf{v}\})
= \sum_{(w,c) \in \mathcal{D}}
\Big[ \log \sigma(\mathbf{u}_w^\top \mathbf{v}_c)
+ \sum_{j=1}^{K} \mathbb{E}_{c_j \sim P_n}\!
\big( \log \sigma(-\mathbf{u}_w^\top \mathbf{v}_{c_j}) \big) \Big],
$$ {#eq-ch03-sgns}

over the two embedding tables $\{\mathbf{u}_w\}$ and $\{\mathbf{v}_c\}$; the first
term rewards observed pairs, the second penalizes sampled non-pairs, and
$\sigma$ is the logistic sigmoid. The quantity being maximized is a per-pair
log-likelihood, so SGNS is a maximum-likelihood estimator of a two-class
discriminator, not a loss to be minimized in the usual sense. Levy and Goldberg
show that the optimum of (@eq-ch03-sgns) satisfies an implicit factorization: for each
observed pair the inner product equals a shifted pointwise mutual information
[Levy & Goldberg, @levy2014neural],

$$
\mathbf{u}_w^\top \mathbf{v}_c
= \operatorname{PMI}(w,c) - \log K,
\qquad
\operatorname{PMI}(w,c) = \log \frac{p(w,c)}{p(w)\,p(c)},
$$ {#eq-ch03-sgns-pmi}

where $p(w,c)$, $p(w)$, and $p(c)$ are the empirical pair and marginal
probabilities induced by the corpus. The step from (@eq-ch03-sgns) to (@eq-ch03-sgns-pmi) is
the stationary condition of the per-pair logistic loss: at the optimum the model's
implied conditional $\sigma(\mathbf{u}_w^\top\mathbf{v}_c)$ matches the empirical
ratio of observed to sampled co-occurrence, which rearranges to the shift
$-\log K$; increasing the number of negatives therefore shifts every cell of the
factorized matrix by a constant, which is why $K$ is held fixed when comparing
embeddings [@levy2014neural]. This identity links the word2vec family back to the
spectral methods above: SGNS is a low-rank factorization of a shifted PMI matrix,
and it fails to distinguish relations whose PMI values coincide.

## GloVe

GloVe dispenses with sampling and instead fits a linear relation to global
co-occurrence counts. With $X_{ij}$ the number of times word $j$ occurs in the
context of word $i$, GloVe minimizes

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{GloVe}}
= \sum_{i,j} f(X_{ij})
\left( \mathbf{w}_i^\top \tilde{\mathbf{w}}_j + b_i + \tilde{b}_j - \log X_{ij} \right)^2,
$$ {#eq-ch03-glove}

over the word vectors $\mathbf{w}_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the context vectors
$\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_j \in \mathbb{R}^d$, and the scalar biases $b_i, \tilde{b}_j$,
where $f$ is a weighting function that downweights very frequent pairs while
keeping low-count pairs informative [@pennington2014glove]. (@eq-ch03-glove) is
minimized, and its minimizer sets
$\mathbf{w}_i^\top\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_j = \log X_{ij} - b_i - \tilde{b}_j$, so the
biases absorb frequency effects and the final embedding is typically
$\mathbf{w}_i + \tilde{\mathbf{w}}_i$. The assumptions are that the log of
co-occurrence is bilinear in the two embeddings and that $X_{ij}=0$ entries carry
no information (they are dropped); the objective is therefore undefined on
zero-count pairs and must be trained only on observed cells.

## node2vec

Shallow methods transfer to graphs by treating graph walks as sentences and
vertices as words. node2vec generates second-order random walks controlled by
return and in-out parameters $p$ and $q$, then maximizes the SGNS objective
(@eq-ch03-sgns) over the (vertex, context) pairs in those walks [@grover2016node2vec].
The parameters interpolate between breadth-first walks that preserve community
structure ($q>1$) and depth-first walks that preserve structural roles ($q<1$).
The earlier DeepWalk algorithm uses uniform random walks with a similar objective
[@perozzi2014deepwalk], and LINE optimizes first- and second-order proximity
objectives separately [@tang2015line]. GraphSAGE generalizes the idea to inductive
settings by learning aggregator functions rather than a fixed table of node
vectors [@hamilton2017inductive]. Chapter 10 treats these graph-specific methods in
full.

# Autoencoders and Variational Autoencoders

Shallow objectives scale poorly to continuous inputs such as expression profiles
or structures, where the prediction targets are not discrete vocabulary items.
Reconstruction-based models replace prediction with an information bottleneck.

::: {.callout-note}
## Definition
**Autoencoder.** An autoencoder is a pair of functions
$f_\phi: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^k$ (encoder) and
$g_\theta: \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^d$ (decoder) with parameters $\phi$ and
$\theta$, trained so that the composition $g_\theta \circ f_\phi$ reconstructs its
input. The bottleneck activation $f_\phi(\mathbf{x})$ is the embedding.
:::

A basic autoencoder minimizes the reconstruction loss

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{AE}}(\phi, \theta)
= \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left\lVert \mathbf{x}_i - g_\theta\!\left(f_\phi(\mathbf{x}_i)\right) \right\rVert_2^2,
$$ {#eq-ch03-ae}

over $\phi$ and $\theta$; the bottleneck width $k < d$ forces compression and the
squared error is the negative log-likelihood under a Gaussian decoder
[@hinton2006reducing]. If $f_\phi$ and $g_\theta$ are linear with tied weights, the
optimum of (@eq-ch03-ae) recovers the PCA subspace of (@eq-ch03-pca) by the Eckart--Young
theorem [@eckart1936approximation]; nonlinear encoders therefore learn a curved
manifold. Denoising autoencoders improve the representation by requiring recovery
of a clean input $\mathbf{x}$ from a corrupted copy $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$, which
prevents the identity map and encourages robustness to noise
[@vincent2008extracting]. The failure mode to guard against is trivial
memorization: with $k\ge d$ or overly powerful decoders, (@eq-ch03-ae) is minimized by
the identity, so compression and noise injection are essential.

The variational autoencoder (VAE) turns the deterministic bottleneck into a
distribution and trains a generative model. With prior $p(\mathbf{z})$, likelihood
$p_\theta(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{z})$, and approximate posterior
$q_\phi(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{x})$, the VAE maximizes the evidence lower bound
(ELBO):

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{VAE}}(\theta, \phi)
= \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{x})}
\!\left[ \log p_\theta(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{z}) \right]
- D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left( q_\phi(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{x}) \,\Vert\, p(\mathbf{z}) \right)
\;\leq\; \log p_\theta(\mathbf{x}),
$$ {#eq-ch03-vae}

where the first term rewards accurate reconstruction, the second term is the
Kullback--Leibler divergence between the approximate posterior and the prior, and
reparameterization makes the bound differentiable [@kingma2014auto]. (@eq-ch03-vae) is maximized over the decoder parameters $\theta$ and encoder parameters
$\phi$. The bound itself is immediate from Jensen's inequality, because

$$
\log p_\theta(\mathbf{x})
= \log \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x})}\!\left[
\frac{p_\theta(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{z})\,p(\mathbf{z})}{q_\phi(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x})}
\right]
\;\geq\;
\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x})}\!\left[\log p_\theta(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{z})\right]
- D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q_\phi(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x})\,\Vert\,p(\mathbf{z})\right),
$$ {#eq-ch03-elbo}

and the gap between the two sides is exactly
$D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_\phi(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x})\,\Vert\,p_\theta(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x}))$,
which vanishes only when the approximate posterior equals the true posterior. Thus
the ELBO is reconstruction minus a KL regularizer, and the two terms compete: a
flexible $q_\phi$ that matches the prior earns a small KL penalty but may ignore
$\mathbf{x}$, whereas a $q_\phi$ that is informative about $\mathbf{x}$ helps
reconstruction but pays KL. In the extreme of *posterior collapse*, the KL term
dominates and $q_\phi(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x})\approx p(\mathbf{z})$, so the latent
code carries no information about the input. The latent mean serves as the
embedding. Because the objective is a proper likelihood, VAEs underpin the
probabilistic single-cell models of Chapter 8; the trade-off is that
reconstruction and the KL term compete, producing blurrier reconstructions than
adversarial or contrastive models.

# Contrastive and Metric Learning

Contrastive objectives learn embeddings by requiring similar items to be close
and dissimilar items to be far apart, without reconstructing inputs.

::: {.callout-note}
## Definition
**Contrastive learning.** Contrastive learning trains an encoder by forming
*positive* pairs (two views or instances that should map nearby) and *negative*
pairs (instances that should map apart), then optimizing a loss over their
similarities in the embedding space.
:::

Contrastive predictive coding introduced the InfoNCE objective, which treats
prediction of a future latent state among negative samples as a
$K$-way classification problem [@vandenoord2018representation]. For an anchor
$\mathbf{x}$, a positive $\mathbf{x}^{+}$, and $K$ negatives $\mathbf{x}^{-}_j$,
drawn jointly, with encoder $f_\theta$ and temperature $\tau > 0$, the loss is

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{InfoNCE}}(\theta)
= -\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[
\log \frac{\exp\!\left(f_\theta(\mathbf{x})^\top f_\theta(\mathbf{x}^{+}) / \tau\right)}
{\exp\!\left(f_\theta(\mathbf{x})^\top f_\theta(\mathbf{x}^{+}) / \tau\right)
+ \sum_{j=1}^{K} \exp\!\left(f_\theta(\mathbf{x})^\top f_\theta(\mathbf{x}^{-}_j) / \tau\right)}
\right],
$$ {#eq-ch03-infonce}

where $\tau$ controls the sharpness of the distribution and the ratio is the
model's estimate of whether the positive is more compatible with the anchor than
the negatives. (@eq-ch03-infonce) is minimized over the encoder parameters
$\theta$ (and any projection head); for any critic the loss satisfies

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{InfoNCE}}(\theta)
\;\geq\; \log (K+1) - I\!\left(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{x}^{+}\right),
$$ {#eq-ch03-infonce-mibound}

with equality when $f_\theta$ realizes the optimal density ratio
$p(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{+})/(p(\mathbf{x})p(\mathbf{x}^{+}))$
[@vandenoord2018representation]. Minimizing (@eq-ch03-infonce) therefore maximizes the
right-hand side, i.e. a lower bound on the mutual information between anchor and
positive; the bound improves with more negatives $K$ and with a critic that
approximates the true density ratio, which is why batch size and negative-sampling
strategy matter. The bound is also the failure mode: when negatives are chosen
from the same class as the positive (*false negatives*), the true mutual
information is penalized and the learned geometry degrades.

The triplet loss is the metric-learning precursor of the same idea. Given an
anchor $a$, a positive $p$, a negative $n$, and a margin $m > 0$,

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{triplet}}(\theta)
= \sum_{(a,p,n)} \max\!\left(
\left\lVert f_\theta(a) - f_\theta(p) \right\rVert_2^2
- \left\lVert f_\theta(a) - f_\theta(n) \right\rVert_2^2 + m, \; 0
\right),
$$ {#eq-ch03-triplet}

which is minimized over $\theta$; the margin enforces a fixed gap between the
positive and negative squared distances, and the loss is zero once the positive is
closer than the negative by at least $m$ [@schroff2015facenet]. Large-margin
nearest-neighbor methods define the same geometry with a learned Mahalanobis
metric [@weinberger2009distance]. The requirement is that at least one negative be
sampled per anchor; without informative negatives the objective is trivially
satisfied and the encoder may collapse all points to a single location.

SimCLR popularized a simplified recipe: apply two augmentations to each input,
treat the two views as a positive pair, and use the remaining batch members as
negatives with a temperature-scaled cross-entropy loss, i.e. (@eq-ch03-infonce) with
$f_\theta$ composed of the encoder and a small projection head [@chen2020simple].
This "augment, embed, contrast" pattern is central to biological foundation models
because it needs no labels and no reconstruction, and because domain-specific
augmentations — reverse-complementing DNA, masking residues, perturbing structures
— encode biological invariances directly into the objective.

# Self-Supervised Pretraining, Fine-Tuning, and Linear Probing

Contrastive and reconstruction objectives are instances of self-supervised
learning, in which supervision is derived from the data itself rather than from
labels.

::: {.callout-note}
## Definition
**Self-supervised pretraining.** Self-supervised pretraining trains an encoder on
a large unlabeled corpus using a surrogate objective built from the data, after
which the encoder is adapted to downstream tasks. *Fine-tuning* updates all
parameters on labeled data; *linear probing* freezes the encoder and fits only a
linear classifier on its embeddings.
:::

The standard pipeline has three stages. First, the encoder is pretrained on a
large corpus with a self-supervised objective. Second, the encoder is either
frozen (probing) or updated (fine-tuning) on a smaller labeled dataset. Third, the
frozen or adapted embeddings feed a downstream head for classification,
regression, or retrieval. Formally, with a frozen encoder $f_\theta$ and a linear
head $g_{\mathrm{head}}(\mathbf{z}) = \operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{W}_{\text{head}}\mathbf{z})$
for $\mathbf{W}_{\text{head}}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times k}$ and $C$ classes, probing minimizes the
cross-entropy $\sum_i -\log g_{\mathrm{head}}(f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_i))_{y_i}$ over
$\mathbf{W}_{\text{head}}$ alone, whereas fine-tuning minimizes the same loss over $\theta$ and
$\mathbf{W}_{\text{head}}$ jointly. Linear probing therefore measures what is already linearly
accessible in the representation, whereas fine-tuning measures what the encoder
can learn given the task; a large gap between the two indicates that the
representation encodes the relevant information but not in a linearly separable
form.

::: {#fig-pretrain}
**Figure description.** The pretrain → adapt → evaluate pipeline. A large
unlabeled corpus (sequences, structures, graphs) feeds a self-supervised
objective (contrastive, reconstruction, or masked prediction) that trains an
encoder. The trained encoder is then either frozen and paired with a linear probe,
or fine-tuned jointly with a task head on labeled data. Both routes produce a
downstream prediction, and the difference between probe and fine-tune accuracy is
interpreted as the linear accessibility of the pretrained features.
:::

# Masked Language Modeling for Biological Sequences

The dominant self-supervised objective for sequence models is masked language
modeling (MLM). A fraction of input tokens is replaced with a mask token, and the
model predicts the masked tokens from their context:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{MLM}}(\theta)
= - \sum_{i \in \mathcal{M}}
\log p_\theta\!\left( x_i \mid \mathbf{x}_{\setminus \mathcal{M}} \right),
$$ {#eq-ch03-mlm}

where $\mathcal{M}$ is the set of masked positions, $x_i$ is the original token at
position $i$, $\mathbf{x}_{\setminus \mathcal{M}}$ denotes the observed tokens
(left and right context), and $p_\theta$ is the model's softmax distribution over
the token vocabulary [@devlin2019bert]. (@eq-ch03-mlm) is minimized over
$\theta$, and it is a sum of per-position cross-entropies: the model treats masked
positions as conditionally independent given the observed tokens, which is an
approximation, since true token dependencies need not factorize, and it is why
masking rates and the choice of which positions to mask affect the quality of the
resulting embeddings. Unlike the causal objective of a generative language model,
MLM uses bidirectional context, and the resulting [CLS] or pooled hidden states
serve as sequence embeddings.

The recipe transfers wherever tokens can be defined. DNABERT applies MLM over
overlapping $k$-mer tokens to the human genome [@ji2021dnabert]; protein language
models such as ESM apply it to amino-acid sequences and show that the learned
representations expose structure and function [@rives2021biological], and
ProtTrans/ProtBERT and ProtT5 do the same across large protein corpora
[@elnaggar2022prottrans]. Masked prediction is attractive for biological sequence
data because it requires only raw sequences, tolerates the enormous unlabeled
corpora available, and produces context-dependent embeddings in which the same
residue receives different vectors in different neighborhoods. Chapters 4, 5, and
7 examine the modality-specific instantiations in detail.

# Learning Objectives at a Glance

The required artifact for this chapter is a single view of how each method couples
an objective to the structure it optimizes. The table below is illustrative of the
taxonomy and is not a performance comparison.

| Method | Loss (equation) | What it optimizes |
|:--|:--|:--|
| PCA / SVD | Projected variance, least-squares residual (@eq-ch03-pca) | Preserved variance; linear subspace |
| Laplacian eigenmaps | $\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{Y}^\top \mathbf{L} \mathbf{Y})$ under $\mathbf{Y}^\top \mathbf{D} \mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{I}_k$ (@eq-ch03-laplacian) | Smoothness over a graph's edges |
| SGNS | Negative-sampling log-likelihood (@eq-ch03-sgns); shifted PMI (@eq-ch03-sgns-pmi) | Co-occurrence predictability |
| GloVe | Weighted least squares on $\log X_{ij}$ (@eq-ch03-glove) | Global co-occurrence ratios |
| node2vec | SGNS (@eq-ch03-sgns) on biased random walks | Node community and role structure |
| Autoencoder | Squared reconstruction (@eq-ch03-ae) | Compressed, faithful representation |
| VAE | ELBO (@eq-ch03-vae), (@eq-ch03-elbo) | Likelihood of data under a latent prior |
| InfoNCE / CPC | Contrastive classification (@eq-ch03-infonce); MI bound (@eq-ch03-infonce-mibound) | Mutual information between views |
| Triplet loss | Margin-based ranking loss (@eq-ch03-triplet) | Relative metric geometry |
| MLM / BERT | Masked-token cross-entropy (@eq-ch03-mlm) | Bidirectional contextual prediction |

A second artifact, the pretrain → adapt → evaluate pipeline, is shown in
@fig-pretrain. Together the table and the figure show the recurring motif of this
chapter: an embedding is only as good as the objective and the invariances that
objective encodes.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key Takeaways
- Every embedding is the solution to an optimization problem; the objective, not
  the architecture, determines what the coordinates encode.
- PCA is the best linear reconstruction (@eq-ch03-pca) and the baseline every learned
  embedding should be compared against.
- Shallow prediction methods (SGNS, GloVe, node2vec) are implicitly matrix
  factorizations of co-occurrence statistics; SGNS factorizes a shifted PMI
  matrix (@eq-ch03-sgns-pmi).
- Autoencoders compress deterministically (@eq-ch03-ae), while VAEs optimize a
  probabilistic bound whose reconstruction and KL terms compete (@eq-ch03-elbo).
- Contrastive objectives such as InfoNCE (@eq-ch03-infonce) and SimCLR dominate
  biological foundation models because they need no labels and encode domain
  invariances through augmentation.
- Linear probing measures what is already accessible in a representation;
  fine-tuning measures what the encoder can additionally learn.
:::

## Further Reading

- Bengio, Courville, and Vincent, *Representation Learning: A Review and New
  Perspectives* (2013) [@bengio2013representation] — the conceptual frame for
  learned representations.
- Levy and Goldberg, *Neural Word Embedding as Implicit Matrix Factorization*
  (2014) [@levy2014neural] — the bridge between word2vec and spectral methods.
- Kingma and Welling, *Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes* (2014)
  [@kingma2014auto] — the primary source for the VAE objective.
- van den Oord, Li, and Vinyals, *Representation Learning with Contrastive
  Predictive Coding* (2018) [@vandenoord2018representation] — the origin of
